P1.evidence: The setter handoff was used better here than anywhere else in the batch — not just acknowledged at the open ('already got some information from Kim, but I just want to have a general conversation with you') but drawn on twice mid-call to show the prospect he had been listened to: 'of course, Kim already mentioned it as well. Like it's more like the chronic side, right?' and 'from what Kim told me, it sounds like it's a hard time in the morning to get started.' That is precisely the 'so they feel seen' intent. Agreement was sought and given, and the open question ran with the prospect's name. The frame is the thinnest in the batch, however — 'seeing if we can actually help you get to the goals that you have, if not totally fine, I'll point you in the right direction as well' is one part plus the disqualification clause.

P2.evidence: The injury enquiry is the best in the batch: duration asked, a 1-to-10 scale run, the morning-versus-afternoon variation established, the specific functional limitation drawn out (cannot get his leg into his trousers unaided), and a follow-up question that surfaced the whole surgical history — 'Any other surgeries you should know about?' — producing the hernia and the knee on top of the back and four shoulders. Training and diet were equally thorough, down to rep schemes, rest intervals, the fasting attempt, the coffee and the daily peanut butter. Against that, P2a is a total miss: age, height and weight were never asked and are not recoverable from the transcript at all. Health conditions were only partially covered — surgeries yes, but no question about current conditions, medications or hereditary history, and the high LDL cholesterol arrived from his wife and was never picked up. Sleep and daily energy were both absent, in a call with a man describing constant inflammation and chronic pain.

P3.evidence: The bridge question ran well and with a genuinely good setup: 'why is it for you so important to actually get that nailed down and just get rid of that? The reason I'm asking that is there's so many people out there that are just okay and they say it's part of becoming old and they just accept it.' That produced hiking, the children and the grandchildren. The can't-do question was covered thoroughly across the call — socks, trousers, holding grandchildren, hiking. Mobility and flexibility were explored in real detail. The recap ran with an explicit invitation to correct it. Where it falls short is the deep drive: 'who else does that impact?' was never asked, and the family material surfaced only because the prospect volunteered it and because his wife was physically present doing the emotional work the question is meant to do. The aesthetic and functional opener was skipped, reasonably, since pain relief was named as the sole goal in the first thirty seconds.

P4.evidence: The strongest sequence in the call and the moment that created most of its value. The rep asked cleanly — 'the reason I'm asking is just to sort of see if you've tried things already, like what worked, what didn't work?' — and surfaced yoga, a YouTube mobility channel and wall-based flexibility work, all of which produced gains that reverted within days. The prospect stated the root-cause question himself: 'why do I keep doing it if I'm just going to go back to where I was?' The rep then answered it with the static-versus-dynamic stretching distinction, which landed hard enough that the wife wrote it down and read it back: 'I hadn't really thought about that as it just being a stretch, and then it comes back. Whereas if it's a dynamic movement, it's building the muscle long, it's lengthening.' Marked down because the actual blocker — a surgically altered spine and a fear of loading it — was never named as the thing in the way, and the 'why can't you stick to it on your own' challenge was absent.

P5.evidence: The projection ran with a horizon attached and produced a usable answer: 'do you feel like if you sort of keep doing it like it's currently going, right, so sort of just toughening up, being okay with it, do you feel like that's going to be very beneficial if you keep doing it for the next 10 years?' — answered 'It won't get me any farther. You know, I'll just be, you know, status quo.' The rep had to rephrase once when the question was misread, which he did well. The settle check was then delivered as a statement for the prospect to agree with rather than asked as a question, and the transcript is degraded at that point. 'Why not?' and the line-in-the-sand question were both absent. For a man who describes himself as desperate, the cost of another ten years at status quo was available and only half-taken.

P6.evidence: The 1-to-10 check was correctly placed before the number and correctly isolated cost — 'unlike a scale from one to ten... The only thing that you still want to know is the price aspect. Whereabouts do you think that you're at?' But it never produced a rating. The answer came back as 'I'm kind of really interested. My interest is pretty well, pretty high right now', and the rep accepted it without pressing for the number the question exists to produce. No belief question in the scripted form and no all-in isolation question were asked. P6c is a clear miss: he moved to price without a clear yes and while carrying two live blockers — the recourse concern, which only surfaced after the number, and the August start date. The recourse objection in particular was foreseeable and would almost certainly have appeared had the all-in question been put.

P11.evidence: Price and a payment structure were presented but the prospect deferred to a booked follow-up on 30 July with an intended 1 August start, so no payment or onboarding step was reachable.

objection_plays.detail: Triggered by genuine price shock at twice the expected figure. Isolation ran twice and well — once before the number via the 1-to-10 framing, and once after: 'is it like, is it just out of reach? Or is it something like it is something we can figure out?', answered 'No, it's not out of reach.' That is the correct diagnostic and it correctly identified a deliberation problem rather than a capacity one. The break-it-up move ran and produced a structured plan. None of the six financial-picture questions ran, which is defensible once 'not out of reach' had been established. The HOW-versus-SHOULD reframe was not used, and no attempt was made to close on the deliberation itself — the rep moved straight to booking a follow-up when the prospect asked for time.

Triggered squarely: 'if it doesn't work, if it's not for me, I don't have any recourse.' The rep diagnosed the need precisely — 'you just want to make sure that it is actually working within like the first month?' — and solved it structurally with a 30-day exit, which the prospect accepted. Commercially effective, and the only objection in this call that was genuinely resolved. But none of the scripted play ran: no 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', no pain-versus-pleasure question, no bridge, no plane analogy, no 'burned before' frame. The fear was answered with a term change rather than addressed, and the term change is itself flagged as an improvisation outside the offer.

Present in substance — the prospect ruled out starting before 1 August because of a two-week US trip. None of the play ran: no 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'what if all you had to do was show up'. The rep accepted the constraint immediately and booked a return call. Recorded as a miss for scoring consistency, but it should be read as reasonable judgement rather than a failure: the prospect will be travelling between locations without access to kettlebells, and pushing a start date into that would have set the programme up to fail.

Script gap, and the third appearance of the clinical-fit gap already logged in the playbook. The presentation here is the most severe in the corpus: five surgeries including a 2020 spinal operation, chronic daily pain, a self-diagnosis of degenerative disc disease and arthritis obtained from ChatGPT rather than a clinician, high LDL cholesterol raised by a nurse, and an explicit statement that he fears loading his spine. The rep came closer than anyone else in the batch to a screen — he disclaimed 'we're not clinical people, right?' and asked 'have you gone to a specialist with anything?' — but on hearing 'I haven't really been to a specialist' he rephrased his own question away from the topic, never suggested obtaining clearance, and followed the disclaimer immediately with 'We have seen it work with so many people. So we know it works.' There is no scripted step that would have required him to stop, and so he did not.

notes: The best setter handoff and the best injury history in the batch, and a genuinely valuable moment of coaching in Past Attempts where the static-versus-dynamic explanation answered a question the prospect had been carrying for years. Two things need correcting. The rep asked the right clinical question — the only time it happens in these twelve calls — and then walked away from the answer; 'I haven't really been to a specialist' from a man with five surgeries and a fear of loading his spine is a stop, not a detail. And he reached price with no rating from his own 1-to-10 check and two unresolved blockers, then solved the one that surfaced by inventing a 30-day exit rather than by having isolated it beforehand. Coach on treating an unscreened surgical history as a hard gate, and on requiring an actual number before moving to the investment.
